finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /me copies the entire request body onto the authenticated user object and persists it, so any user can set privileged or protected fields (e.g. role, isAdmin, id, email verification, balance) on their own account. Only the sibling /me/profile route restricts fields to displayName and bio, which shows the intended whitelist was skipped here.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled JSON body of PUT /me from any authenticated user (req.body)
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) followed by req.store.save(req.user), which persists arbitrary attributes on the user record

trace.note: PUT /me handler reads req.body with no field filtering
Object.assign merges all body keys into req.user, including privileged fields such as role or isAdmin
Updated user is returned in the response, confirming the change

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, schema validation, or field denylist in this file. Only one file exists in the repo, so I could not see upstream middleware that might filter req.body. The /me/profile route at lines 10-15 does destructure to an allowlist, which contrasts with /me. Object.assign does not set prototype via __proto__ from JSON.parse keys as an own property, so prototype pollution is not claimed. Impact depends on what fields the user model treats as privileged, which is not visible in this repo.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no filtering, and users.js:6 persists it, so any authenticated user can overwrite arbitrary fields on their own record. The /me/profile route at users.js:11-12 does use an allowlist, which shows the intended behavior. The repo contains only users.js, so upstream middleware can't be ruled out, but nothing in the code blocks this. Which fields count as privileged depends on the user model, which isn't visible.
